I don't follow. If someone isn't moving relative to me, from my point of view they are occupying a single point in space while occupying multiple points in time. So then why shouldn't they also be able to occupy multiple points in space while occupying a single point in time? If time is a dimension, what's special about time that this can't be done?

Because you cannot know all the other ways a particle is moving or being influenced. You can only know how it moves relative to your inertial reference frames. You can only know how it moves relative to your inertial reference frames.

Exactly. And I'm seeing that he doesn't move relative to me. Not only that, but I also have no points of reference to tell me that either of us are moving at all. You either don't understand or you are just nitpicking, so I will simply reword the question to fit the thought experiment I have just laid out for you.

Again, we are speaking in terms of a thought experiment. You have two people who are not moving relative to each other. They cannot see any points of reference that would reveal motion, so that they both appear stationary to each other and to themselves.

The question is this: If time is a dimension, what is special about it such that to an observer, you could occupy multiple points in time while apparently occupying a single point in space, but you can't apparently occupy multiple points in space while occupying a single point in time?

Being nitpicky in this situation is important. Time is not a dimension. It is a dimensionless scalar and consequence of differential position. When motion is measured in a relative way, such as with Newtonian Inertial Reference frames, the output is a relative measurement. When time is measured with an absolute reference frame, such as from the big bang, the output of the function is an absolute measurement. However, because we are trapped within a relative reference frame the only measurements that make sense to our limited data inputs is relative measurements. This idea of occupying multiple points in time is an error. Particles occupy a single point in time, but the different frames from which the particle is measured give different views on the same point.

I can get on board with viewing time as a dimensionless scalar because that's what makes classical sense, however I was under the impression that Einstein overturned that. You will still find top physicists today referring to it as a very real dimension.

To me the key here is that our progression through space and time appears to be shared between the two. For example, if you are progressing through a 2 dimensional plane, your motion through the horizontal is related to your motion through the vertical such that as you change direction to go more horizontal while going the same speed, your progression in the vertical will be slowed. This works the same way with space and time. As you speed up through space, your progression through time slows down relative to things which are moving slower.

Here's one example from Kip Thorne: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mvdlN4H4T54

He describes space and time as being linked in much the same way as the three familiar spacial dimensions are linked to one another.

Particles do in fact occupy multiple points along the timeline, not merely a single point. If this were not the case, you and I would pop out of existence in the next instant. Yet we remain as time marches forward from our perspective, whereas people like Kip and other physicists convey our existence as a fixed piece of geometry in 4 dimensions.
